you need to add them to your CORS configurations ([CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing)](cors.md)) using the parameter `expose_headers`

queries.q: Which configuration does Ruff choose for a file in a nested directory, and how can formatting violations be checked without changing the file?

span.text:
For each file, Ruff uses the "closest" config file in the
directory hierarchy.

`ruff format --check /path/to/file.py` will avoid writing any formatted files back,
and instead exit with a non-zero status code upon detecting any unformatted files.

required_facts.description: Ruff uses the closest configuration file in the directory hierarchy.
ruff format --check does not write and returns nonzero for unformatted files.

queries.q: How does Ruff explicitly inherit another config, and does formatting Python examples inside docstrings require opting in?

span.text:
supports an [`extend`](settings.md#extend) field, which allows you to inherit the settings from another
config file

The Ruff formatter provides an opt-in feature for automatically formatting
Python code examples in docstrings.

required_facts.description: The extend field explicitly inherits another configuration file.
Formatting docstring Python examples is an opt-in feature.

queries.q: Which Ruff config wins when .ruff.toml, ruff.toml and pyproject.toml coexist, and what happens to invalid Python examples when docstring formatting is enabled?

span.text:
If Ruff detects multiple configuration files in the same directory, the `.ruff.toml` file will take
precedence over the `ruff.toml` file, and the `ruff.toml` file will take precedence over
the `pyproject.toml` file.

If a code example is recognized and treated as Python, the Ruff formatter will
automatically skip it if the code does not parse as valid Python or if the
reformatted code would produce an invalid Python program.

required_facts.description: Precedence is .ruff.toml, then ruff.toml, then pyproject.toml.
Ruff skips unparseable or invalidly reformatted Python docstring examples.

queries.q: When Ruff receives a config directly through --config, how are its relative paths resolved, and at what granularity do fmt on/off comments suppress formatting?

any relative paths in that configuration file (like `exclude` globs or
    `src` paths) are resolved relative to the _current_ working directory.
`# fmt: on` and `# fmt: off` comments are enforced at the statement level:

required_facts.description: Relative paths in an explicitly supplied configuration are resolved against the current working directory.
fmt on/off suppression operates at statement level.

queries.q: How can Ruff enforce exclusions for files explicitly passed on the command line, and why can a formatted file still trigger E501?

span.text:
Files that are passed to `ruff` directly are always analyzed, regardless of the above criteria, 
unless [`force-exclude`](settings.md#force-exclude) is also enabled (via CLI or settings file).

the formatter only makes a best-effort attempt to wrap lines at the configured
[`line-length`](settings.md#line-length). As such, formatted code _may_ exceed the line length,
leading to [`line-too-long`](rules/line-too-long.md) (`E501`) errors.

required_facts.description: force-exclude is required to enforce exclusion on directly supplied files.
Formatting is best effort about line length, so E501 may remain.

queries.q: How does uv run keep project dependencies synchronized, and why should pytest that needs the installed project use it instead of uvx?

This protects against a compromise of PyPI or the HTTPS certificate chain. It

Installing directly from a source
distribution will make pip build a wheel, regardless of whether there is a
matching cached wheel.

required_facts.description: Package hashes protect against index/certificate-chain compromise and changed package bytes under the same version.
Installing the source distribution directly forces wheel building despite a matching cached wheel.

queries.q: Is a pip wheelhouse necessarily portable across operating systems, and are wheels from pip install dot reused from cache across separate runs?

span.text:
Note that such a wheelhouse contains compiled packages, which are typically
OS and architecture-specific, so these archives are not necessarily portable
across machines.

Wheels built from source distributions provided to pip as a direct path (such
as `pip install .`) are not cached across runs

required_facts.description: Wheelhouses may contain OS/architecture-specific compiled packages and need not be portable.
Wheels built from direct local source paths are not cached across separate pip runs.

queries.q: Which pip install flag prevents installing dependencies absent from the pinned requirements, and how can both wheel and HTTP caches be cleared?

span.text:
Performing the installation using
{ref}`--no-deps <install_--no-deps>` would provide an extra dose of insurance
against installing anything not explicitly listed.
`pip cache purge` will clear all files from pip's wheel and HTTP caches.

queries.q: Why should pip-compile run inside the project's virtual environment, and in what order does the source code check default input filenames?

span.text:
`pip-compile` should be run from the same virtual environment as your
project so conditional dependencies that require a specific Python version,
or other environment markers, resolve relative to your project's
environment.

DEFAULT_REQUIREMENTS_FILES = (
    "requirements.in",
    "setup.py",
    "pyproject.toml",
    "setup.cfg",
)

required_facts.description: Run pip-compile in the project's environment so markers and Python-dependent requirements resolve correctly.
Default input priority is requirements.in, setup.py, pyproject.toml, setup.cfg.

queries.q: How does pip-compile use an existing output file to stabilize versions, and what happens if a file is specified as both input and output?

span.text:
When you run `pip-compile`, it reads any existing output file (e.g.,
`requirements.txt`) and uses the versions specified there as constraints.
This ensures that the output is stable -- `pip-compile` will prefer to
use existing pinned versions.

required_facts.description: Existing output pins become constraints and are preferred for stability.
A matching input/output filename raises click.BadArgumentUsage, except the stdout dash.

queries.q: Which packaging tools does pip-sync avoid upgrading or uninstalling, and how does pip-compile pass the configured resolution-round limit to its resolver?

span.text:
`pip-sync` will not upgrade or uninstall packaging tools like
`setuptools`, `pip`, or `pip-tools` itself.
results = resolver.resolve(max_rounds=max_rounds)

pip-compile forwards the round limit through resolver.resolve(max_rounds=max_rounds).

queries.q: What pip-compile flag enables package hashes, and how does its implementation choose between legacy and backtracking resolvers?

span.text:
If you would like to use _Hash-Checking Mode_ available in `pip` since
version 8.0, `pip-compile` offers `--generate-hashes` flag:
resolver_cls = LegacyResolver if resolver_name == "legacy" else BacktrackingResolver

The legacy name selects LegacyResolver; other supported selections use BacktrackingResolver.

queries.q: Which pip-tools requirement files should be version-controlled, and what does the newline helper return if its strategy remains preserve after checking input files?

span.text:
Generally, yes. If you want a reproducible environment installation available
from your source control, then yes, you should commit both `requirements.in`
and `requirements.txt` to source control.

The preserve fallback returns the LF newline string.

queries.q: Which Flask installation extra enables coroutine error handlers, and does registering a handler automatically set the response's HTTP status?

span.text:
Routes, error handlers, before request, after request, and teardown
functions can all be coroutine functions if Flask is installed with the
``async`` extra (``pip install flask[async]``).

The status code of the response will not be set to the handler's code. Make
sure to provide the appropriate HTTP status code when returning a response from
a handler.

required_facts.description: The flask[async] extra enables coroutine views, error handlers, and request hooks.
A handler must explicitly return the appropriate status code.

queries.q: Does a Flask async view free its worker to handle other requests, and how is an exception handler selected if there are code and class registrations?

span.text: Each request still ties up one worker, even for async views.

When Flask catches an exception while handling a request, it is first looked up by code.
If no handler is registered for the code, Flask looks up the error by its class hierarchy; the most specific handler is chosen.

required_facts.description: An async Flask request still occupies one worker.
Flask first checks the HTTP code, then chooses the most specific registered class handler.

queries.q: What happens to unfinished tasks spawned by a Flask async view, and where can an InternalServerError handler find the original uncaught exception?

span.text:
This means any additional
spawned tasks that haven't completed when the async function completes
will be cancelled.
The original error is available as ``e.original_exception``.

required_facts.description: Unfinished tasks are cancelled when the view's event loop stops.
The wrapped original exception is available through e.original_exception.

queries.q: How can a Flask extension decorator support coroutine views, and why can't a blueprint's handler catch a routing-level 404?

span.text:
Extension authors can support async functions by utilising the
:meth:`flask.Flask.ensure_sync` method.

the blueprint cannot handle 404 routing errors
because the 404 occurs at the routing level before the blueprint can be
determined.

required_facts.description: Extension authors can wrap view calls using Flask.ensure_sync.
Routing 404s happen before Flask can determine the blueprint, so its handler cannot handle them.

queries.q: Which framework do Flask's docs suggest considering for a mainly async codebase, and what replaces a registered 500 handler in debug mode?

span.text:
If you have a mainly async codebase it
would make sense to consider `Quart`_.

In debug mode, a handler
for "500 Internal Server Error" will not be used. Instead, the
interactive debugger will be shown.

Debug mode shows the interactive debugger rather than using the 500 error handler.
